transcript:
Contents of this podcast are for educational with entertainment purposes only and do not purport to be internet attended to be financial, legal, accounting, tax, or investment advice.
Investments and strategies that are discussed may not be suitable for you.
Do not take into account your particular investing objectives, financial situation, or needs that are not attended to provide investment advice or recommendations appropriate for you.
Or making any investment trade, consider whether it's suitable for you and consider seeking advice from your financial and investment advisor.
Good evening, everybody.
On behalf of the finance and investment cell at Sri Lanka, College of Commerce, I extend a warm greeting to each and every one of you,
and thank you so much for joining us today for getting.
another thought-provoking speaker session organized by the finance and investment cell of SRCC.
Today, we are absolutely thrilled to have Mr. Mohaneesh Pabrai as our esteemed speaker.
A very warm welcome to you, sir.
We also welcome our esteemed faculty advisor, Dr. Saro Joshi, and thank her for her unwavering support in all our endeavours.
A visionary in finance and philanthropy, sir, has an audacious, entrepreneurial spirit.
He has founded several successful companies and pioneer the Munger Buffett-focused value investing approach.
He is the founder and managing partner of Pabri investment funds and manages over $500 million in assets.
Yet, the impact he has created extends beyond finance.
Being the founder and chairman of the Daksana Foundation, he's transformed the lives of
of thousands of economically and socially disadvantaged but gifted students worldwide by
providing them with world-class educational opportunities. Having mastered the art of
balanced living, he cherishes family, literature and the strategic complexities of duplicate bridge. Being someone who carries
the pursuit of excellence and the power to create lasting change, it is our utmost pleasure to be able to
learn from your wisdom, sir. We are honored to have you and this honestly feels extremely
surreal for all of us. And just want to put it out there, please do excuse us if our
questions are maybe redundant or if they seem like childish curiosities.
A note for the audience, please do put your questions in the chat box and we'll try our best to entertain
them if time permits. Now, given that a good number of our audience today are high school and
college students. We have some questions tailored in that respect, right?
With that said, where do you think investing should be on the list of priorities
for a teenager? All right, Samarth and Urbi and everyone, it's great to be here.
So two score and one year ago, I was a student at SRCCC, and I had joined SRCC, and I had joined SRCC, just like many of you have joined SRCCC. If you are confused about two score and one year ago, maybe because you haven't heard the Gettysburg address of four score and seven years ago.
but two score and one year ago is 41 years.
And that's 1982 when I finished high school and applied to various colleges at Delhi University.
And I was very excited to join Sri Ram.
And that year, there were some very extended strikes at the university.
So I attended for a few weeks and then the whole place shut down for quite a few months.
And my brother and I attended for a few weeks.
I basically applied to U.S. universities, and I switched from commerce to computer
science and then to computer engineering and then to computer engineering and then basically finished my degree in the
in the U.S. And a life trajectory changed, if you will. But I have very fond memories of taking the
U special buses, you know, the few weeks at Sri Ram at DU. So it was, it was wonderful. And in terms
of, I think, investing and teenagers, you know, I think that educational systems around
the world, I think, do a disservice because really kind of, while while we are taught compounding in a mathematical sense,
in math classes, there really is nothing taught in terms of investing and savings and runways
and so on in high schools.
And I think it would be very beneficial because, you know, there are.
there are really three things that matter in terms of ending up being extremely
wealthy over time, even if you have relatively modest earnings over your lifetime.
So the first is, you know, spending less than you earn is, it's really important right from the beginning.
And Charlie Munger says that if you consistently spend 5% more than you earn,
you will have a life of extreme misery.
But if you spend 5% less than what you earn or 10% less than what you earn, you're going to have a very
bountiful life.
So just a small difference there can lead to a huge delta in outcome.
So spending less than you earn is very important, and I wish that was reinforced in high school.
Putting the savings in a low-cost index fund is also a very good idea.
So you don't need to really understand, you know, how to pick stocks or, you know, find out what are good investments or any of that.
Just, you know, buy a low-cost index fund and there are plenty of them available in India.
And the third is the length of the runway, you know, so it's really important to start early and as early as you can and start putting money away.
and basically what's going to end up happening is a few decades later you look to your right
and you look to your left and you left and you left all your peers way behind and life is great.
So yeah, I wish, I wish these basics were part of core high school curriculums around the
world, but sadly they are not.
Okay, sir, moving on to the next question.
What value do you accord to investing in oneself when there are other options of investing in oneself when
when there are other options of investing as well?
for example, if I'm interning and earning a certain stipend, would you advocate for
upskilling or investing in some securities instead?
Also, do you think people ascribe lesser value to self-learning?
Because returns are not exactly as evident as opposed to the many caring examples of how
financial investments can reap healthy profits.
Yeah, well, I mean, I mean, usually an investment in
improving yourself is usually going to deliver the greatest returns and especially if those investments are made
made very early in life. But I think the most important factor is to pursue your passion. So one should not do an
an MBA because it's going to raise your, you know, compensation or, open up more opportunities or any of that.
one should be doing that if one is very passionate about management and, you know, investing, or just in general, commerce and industry in general.
So it is not, it is not easy as a young person to have clarity on what is your calling in life.
and the more time you can spend early in life to try to get clarity on who you are and what, you know, excites you and doesn't excite you and doesn't excite you is really important.
And I think some some clues of that will come to you when you notice that maybe in high school, you're excited about certain classes and certain subjects and certain subjects and not so excited about other classes and other classes and other subjects.
So start spending more time on the things that you're excited about, start thinking about careers, etc, in that direction.
And, and I think the self-learning, I think self-learning is extremely important.
If I, if I look back at my undergraduate, you know, computer engineering degree,
there are really just a couple of forces I can think of that had a huge lifelong impact on me.
One was an elective class I took on public speaking, and I really enjoyed that class and it
was a wonderful. Actually, I just tossed a coin, whether that class or technical writing, and it
turned out public speaking was excellent. So I think, I think to the extent that
you can, because when we go through formal degrees and such, when you look back after five, 10, 10, 15 years,
very little of what you learned during your school days is going to be relevant in the real
world. What is really going to help you a lot in the real world is really going to help you a lot in the real world is
if you go to sleep every day a little wiser than when you woke up and that you make
reading a lifelong activity. And I think it's just like compounding. What happens in 10, 15, 15, 20 years is
that you look to your right, look to your left and your peers are so far behind. And you've gone so far
far ahead. And you didn't go ahead because you just, you know, sprinted really fast. It's more
of a marathon than a sprint, but that distance keeps increasing daily. And
you're enjoying the journey as well. So yeah, definitely, I'd say, invest in yourself through formal degrees and
to self-learning. I mean, we have a limited time on planet Earth, you know, try to make the most
of it and try to enjoy the journey. So I think I just have a follow-up question. So you say we should,
you should become wiser every day and find what our true calling is, what drives us, right?
But do you think one should do anything at all for the sake of it or do you think, like you said, inherent motivation and
inclination should drive all our endeavors? And I'm asking this against the backdrop that, you know,
while crafting one's career, there are several options and opportunities that may, you know,
fast track one's career, right? But they, they, at the core of it, they have a hollow impact on
one's personal growth. So do you think those opportunities are maybe worth
pursuing or is it just the become wiser everyday approach you would maybe suggest? Well, you know, there are
practicalities in the sense that basically when we pursue degrees, we don't have a lot of choice about, you know,
what what courses we take and what professors we get and which classes are interesting, which class
are not. So a lot of that is going to be hit or miss. We don't have a whole
lot of choice in there because, you know, the only choice we have is whether we do the degree
or not. So try to make sure that the degree is as closely aligned to what you're interested in.
And I think, I think beyond that, I think if you follow your nose, it will lead, it will lead to great
things. I think that what I've always found is that when I'm really curious about something
and I'll go down a rabbit hole of trying to figure it out many times it's extremely
rewarding. In fact, I ended up in the investment business just because I accidentally picked up a book
on investing to read on a flight from Heath Road to Chicago. And I really picked it up at
random and I never worked in the industry. I didn't have degrees in finance and so on. And it was
really that that book led me down a rabbit hole of other readings and other books
and other writings and other writings. And here we are, you know. So, so I think, I think it's really important
to to pursue what you are really interested in and pursue it to the fullest extent that you can.
Right. Thank you so much for that answer, sir. So you're evidently an advocate of
You say it's the approach of doing businesses that, a business that guarantees an upside
without the possibility of a downside. Now, another word that really fascinates me is Jugaad, right? And I just
want to understand from you, what do you think Jugaar's relevance is for an entrepreneur and an entrepreneur's
journey, really? Well, I think the Indian word Jugaad is kind of difficult to directly translate.
But I think most of you know what what it means.
And yes, absolutely, I mean, hacks in life are really important.
And when we're, you know, when I'm looking at a particular business or a particular industry, what, what I'm, you know, the data set is very large.
So when you're, when you're looking at a, you know, some industry, I think just the amount of
information and what, what is going on is can be daunting. But the important thing is that you have to get to
get to the three or four important factors that will drive most of the outcome
and the result of that investment or of that business. And that's where a lot of the Jigar and hacks come in.
So you have to be sensitive to how can you accelerate the process if you can. There's,
there's obviously the base path that you can take, which is, you can, you can, you can, you can accelerate the process if you can. There's obviously
the base path that you can take, which is you can read a lot of historic annual
reports and you can read a lot of historic transcripts and you look at a lot of things the company has said in
the past, etc. You can read industry reports and you can read competitors annual reports and all of those
things over time will will give you a picture in your head of what's going on and what's important
and so on, it can be accelerated sometimes when if you can read something that someone else
has written about the business or the industry where they've digested a lot of facts already.
And so it can accelerate the learning, but you have to be careful that you're kind of reading
the right stuff or weighting the right stuff in the right amount of weightage that should
be given. So basically, I would say that in investing,
What is really important is that we started a very large data set.
And what you need to end up with is two, three, four factors that are etched in your brain that are going to drive outcome and why those factors are going to likely to work out in a certain way.
Now, the reality of investing is that it's a high error rate.
So even when we do all of that, because businesses are uncertain, we may have 30, 30, 40, 50 percent of the time that we're just wrong.
And that's okay, you know, we learn and keep moving on. But if you're right half the time
and hang on and so on, life will end up, I mean, the end result will be just fine. No issues. No issues.
Thank you, sir. Being a global investor, what's the India story that you see?
What is the future that you envision for the people of India? And what would you
probably say to somebody who wishes to settle abroad?
maybe like better prospects. So just an add-on, what do you think or how do you
envision your life or your life or your career would be had you probably stayed in Shira when not gone to
U.S.? Yeah, you know, let me take the second question first and then I'll get to Poovi's question.
So when when I was in India, in high school, et cetera, I changed a lot of different
schools, moved a lot of different places. But I would say none of my classmates or
I, when we were growing up, had ever expected that we would live any part of our life outside India.
That pretty much just wasn't part of the equation. You know, the idea was that you would finish college
and so on. And I lost touch with a lot of my high school friends and so on. And then Facebook
came around and after many decades, I was reunited with many
you know, great. And what I, what I noticed is that more than half of my classmates in the
different schools I went to ended up outside India. It was a very large number.
I had not expected that, but it was a large number. And I think part of the
reason that happened was that if I had gone to Sri Ram, probably what would
have happened is one way or another, I would have probably ended up in the IT field because it was growing
so fast. And, you know, a lot of people were doing like these diploma courses at an IT and so on, so forth.
And there was a huge boom of people coming to the US because there was a large amount of IT jobs that
it opened up outside India. And so probably the likely trajectory may have been
that I may have ended up in the U.S. and many years later with a somewhat different trajectory than
where I ended up. So, but I think, I think that when we look at the situation today, I think the
situation today is a little bit different in the sense that, you know, the IITs when they were
graduating a lot of students in the 70s and 80s and maybe even in the early 90s, they
just weren't a lot of opportunities in India. So a large portion of those folks ended up going for
master's degrees in the U.S. and they ended up staying and so on. I think today the opportunity set in India
is very different. It's very significant. A lot of multinationals have come into India, a lot of
Indian companies have grown a lot and they're pretty world-class in terms of how they operate and the opportunities they offer.
And at the same time, if I look at a place like the U.S., the immigration situation is such a mess over here that, you know, for people coming on a work visa, sometimes, at least on paper, it looks like it would take 70 or 80 years to get a green card, you know, following the backlogs and waiting lists and all that.
which is ridiculous, actually.
I think the big strength of the U.S.
has been that it's attracted talent from all over the world
and it's built the country.
And I wish the U.S. would fix its immigration system.
Canada has a good system.
Australia has a good system.
Singapore has a good system.
So many other countries are, in fact, gaining what the U.S. is losing at, which is
unfortunate for my vantage point.
But I think looking at it from the point of view of being in India, I think probably the best way to make the decision is in terms of lifestyle and in terms of family and, in terms of family and, you know, what your personal preferences are and personal aspirations are.
But I think there's a lot of opportunities in India and there's also a lot of opportunities outside India.
So I think at this point, it's up to the individual.
Right.
So I just want to go back to the youth investing perspective, right?
Do you think behavioral finance is maybe more important for teenagers when they start
their investing journey?
Because as I see, the technical aspects of investing, you know, ratios, analyzing financial statements,
valuation, etc., can be picked up eventually too.
but is ingraining and investing temperament more important in the youth years?
And if so, how do you think the youth can learn about the psychology of investing?
Yeah, so I think there's a, there's a pretty big demarcation that happens between,
so one can do extremely well by just being a passive investor, you know, just investing in
index funds and so on, and one never needs to study a business or any of that.
And you'll end up with a great result.
Now, if you decide to cross over to the other side, where you actually want to analyze
businesses and figure out investing and buy stocks and all of that, I think that is a very different game.
and probably there's no better way to master it than to take arrows
in your back.
So as you invest, as you make mistakes, you should endeavor to learn from those mistakes, and you should endeavor to learn a lot
from other people's mistakes.
So I think when you, when you move from passive investing or, you know, index investing to,
you know, active management and such, you have to have to have a framework.
So you start with a framework.
So you start with a framework.
So the first few pieces of the framework is how many stocks does your temperament say that you
should hold?
You know, are you comfortable at five or 10 or 20 or 30?
So that needs to fit.
that needs to fit, you know, what your temperaments, et cetera.
The second is that many aspects of investing cannot be taught.
They are inborn traits that either exist or don't.
So if one has the natural tendency of a hyperactive trader who's going in and out of positions several times
a day, it may be difficult to transform that person into someone who buys, you know,
one stock a year, for example, and holds them for 10, 20, 30 years.
I think that's, so I think that's, so I think, I think, knowing your temperament and knowing your aptitude and
comfort level and style is really important.
So you start with some baseline of some things you read and figure out what kind of seems to be
the, and I think reading everything you can that's been put out by Warren Buffett and
Charlie Bunger and all the Berkshire Hathaway meetings which are online at now at Buffett.c.c.com,
which is a tremendous resource, hundreds of hours of video to greatest investors ever, is a great
place to try to understand what your framework should be.
And, and, yeah, then the, you know, the notion of behavioral finance versus, you know, the
of behavioral finance versus, you know, the quantitative stuff, all that kind of naturally
falls into place once you have a framework that you can work with. And you need to come up with something
that fits for you and can work for you and can work for you.
Take it from there.
Just to follow up to that, sir, if you were to give percentages as to why investors make mistakes,
because of their temperament or emotions versus actual stop picking.
What do you think that percentage would look like?
And also, do investors lose less?
I'm not saying make more.
But do they lose less when they don't care in investing?
I'm sorry, can you repeat that last sentence?
Right.
So, so I basically said, do investors lose less when they don't care?
When they don't care?
Yeah, well, yeah, I mean, I think that, I think with investing, the reason the error rate is high is because of, I would say,
primarily two reasons. One is that humans have a tendency to fork, to basically project present circumstances
to infinity. So, for, for example, you know, we have a company in the US called
NVIDIA, and NVIDia just hit a trillion-dollar market cap, and it's up almost like 200% this year in the
first five, five, five, six months. And NVIDia is a great business. It's a great business.
it's at the epicenter of the AI boom.
And a lot of people think that NVIDia will do really well.
I don't have any position in NVIDIA, and I'm not suggesting you should go buy the stock, but I'm just
using it as an example.
So I would say that there's a lot of euphoria around NVIDia.
And if one were to do some type of analysis of a
discounted cash flow model where you look at the earnings of Envidia today and you do some
projections of what you think their earnings are in three years or five years or ten years and then
you discounted back. I think it'd be difficult to justify the billion dollar or trillion dollar market
can be difficult to come up with a future cash flow stream in the next 10
or so that would exceed that. I have no idea what would happen to NVIDIA,
but I would just say that what I have noticed in in equity markets is that they vacillate a lot
between fear and greed. They, they tend to, at times, get very overheated and overvalued,
and they tend to get very depressed at other times. And because it's auction-driven
markets where prices are set by the sentiments of investors.
There's a lot of positive sentiment about NVIDIA. It's a great business. But similar sentiment
existed in early 2000 with Microsoft. And so I remember that when I, when I started my fund in
When I started my fund in 99, one of the first individuals, probably the first 20-30 investors I had,
was a guy who, Indian guy, who had risen quite high in Microsoft and had retired early.
And he was when the very early employees of Microsoft, he knew Bill Gates well,
closely with him and so on. And he, he had made an investment in Pabrii Fund,
and he told me, hey, listen, if you're ever in Seattle, I can introduce you to a bunch of current and former
Microsoft people, and these guys are quite wealthy. They've got a lot of stock options a long time ago.
And some of them may be interested in investing in your fund. And for brii funds
was very new, just like, you know, a couple of million dollars, two, three million
dollars in assets and I said, oh, I'm going to be in Seattle day after tomorrow.
So he said, oh, that's great. So he walked me around Microsoft, introduced me different people,
a bunch of them later, invested with me. But I told many of those individuals I met that their
livelihood was coming from Microsoft. Most of their net worth was in Microsoft stock or
in Microsoft options that had been granted. And when I looked at the
Microsoft market cap at that time in early 2000, it was over 600 billion. It was in the top
three most valuable companies in the world at that time. The top three most valuable companies was Cisco,
Microsoft, and General Electric. None of those would have been a great investment.
If you put, you know, a portfolio, one-third each in these three investments. G. E.E.
is basically, for practical purposes, disappeared. Microsoft never saw that 600 billion
market cap for the next 13 years. And in fact, it took a huge drawdown. I mean, the 600 billion went down
to, I think, less than 100 billion or so thereabouts. So it was a huge drawdown. It's now
at a much higher valuation. So it's done really well. But I think from 2000 to 2012 or 2013,
it would have been a very, very rough and bumpy ride.
And I don't know anyone who would have held on to their stock through that ride.
And the NVIDIA situation today, so the history doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme.
And when I look at the NVIDIA situation today, to me, it rhymes a lot with the way Microsoft
was at that time. It was just, you know, so the blue chips, the blue chips, great
business, recovering revenues. How can you do without Word and Windows and Excel and
all of that. And so it's an important, I mean, now, the other thing about investing is
that there are no called strikes. It's a baseball term. You can let a lot of balls go by and there's no
penalty. You only could possibly get a penalty if you try to hit something. So if I don't make an
investment in NVIDIA, and NVIDIA ends up being a $10 trillion company, 10
years from now, I don't really lose anything. Yes, I didn't make that 10x. But what matters is what I actually
invested in, what happened with those things. So, NVDA could be 10 trillion, you know, a few years from now.
It could be a few hundred billion a few years from now. Or even less, we don't know.
And, and so one of the reasons for the error rate is, like I said, people get
caught up in the euphoria up, flavor of the day, fear of missing out, and all of these
of these things. Another reason why there's a high error rate in investing is we are trying to predict
the future trajectory of a business. The future trajectory of a business has so many different
unknowns and variables. A great manager leaves or a great manager comes in or government
regulations change or there were duties which prevented competitors from abroad coming in and those duties go
way. So there are my rate of factors internal to the company, external to the company
that are with competitors that could affect the future outcomes. And so when we are trying to, you know,
look at a business and say, oh, I think five or 10 years from now, this will be worth, you know,
three times what it's work today. That's an exercise that's prone to, by definition,
a high error rate. And so we need to be aware of that. And I
I think that in general, having a strong dose of pessimism, investing in
an interesting art, you need to be a pessimist and an optimist at the same time. You cannot keep two thoughts in
your head at the same time. And if you can do that, then that can work out quite well.
All right, sir. Do you think investing is a privileged concept and also do you think
there's any further scope for democratizing investing. And if that is possible, then how do you
think that we should go about it? Well, the advances that have taken place in investing, for example, we now have,
you know, we can, we can trade from our phones and, and, you know, the apps are pretty good.
The frictional costs are very low. In the U.S., we can trade from our phones and, we can
with zero frictional costs. You don't pay any commissions if you don't want to.
So on the surface, these look like great things. In reality, what would help investors a lot would be Buffett's
rule of the 20 punch card. So Buffett says that if you were allowed to
if you were allowed to only buy 20 stocks in your entire lifetime, you would be really
careful about each stock that you bought because now you only have 19 left and then you
would have 18 left. So, so basically, I think that the ease of trading and the reduction of frictional
costs have actually had probably a negative impact on investors because they've increased, if they've increased
the propensity to go in and out of positions. So if there were the 20 punch card
rule, investors would be helped. If there was a rule, it said that if you invest in a company,
you cannot sell it for at least five years. That would help investors. So it's kind of counterintuitive,
but if you slowed down the activity and slowed down and reduced the number of decisions,
investors would get help.
I just want to go to China for a bit, right? So Radialio has fleshed out in his book
the changing world order that he sees China being the next global superpower displacing the US. Now,
I'll listen to a couple of your interviews where you've reasoned out why you exited Baba, but I want to know
how you look at this thesis from a geopolitical point of view, right? That is, the investing aside,
